html:
The map's label for the peoples of Mexico and Central America around 2000 BCE, near the end of the long shift from foraging to farming. Bands still hunted deer and small game and gathered wild plants, but more and more of them planted.

Maize had been bred from a wild grass, teosinte, in the Balsas River valley of south-western Mexico about 9,000 years ago. For thousands of years its cobs stayed small, and it was one food among many. With beans and squash, the trio later called the Three Sisters, it slowly became the base of the diet.

By about 2000 BCE people in several regions lived in villages and made pottery. Cooking maize with lime, nixtamalisation, made it more nourishing and was in use soon after. On this base the Olmec built the first large centres after 1200 BCE, while maize spread far beyond the region with other maize farmers.
